papers.abstract: Accurate calculations of correlated fermions at low temperatures constitute a major challenge in quantum many-body physics, most notably in the studies of high-$T_c$ superconductivity and ultracold atom optical lattices. Stochastic sampling of tensor-network states offers a promising route to tackle this problem; however, existing schemes have long faced a fundamental dilemma---sampling efficiency and symmetry acceleration \textit{cannot} be achieved simultaneously. Here we propose a perfect Born sampling approach for thermal tensor networks, which performs importance sampling directly from the purified density matrix via the Born rule and incorporates Abelian and non-Abelian symmetries by sampling symmetry quantum numbers. We benchmark the method, realized as both stochastic matrix product states (stoMPS) and stochastic projected entangled pair states (stoPEPS), on large-scale quantum lattice models. Using stoMPS, we accurately simulate the square-lattice Hubbard model on cylinders up to width $W=10$, and study the triangular-lattice Hubbard model down to $T/t = 1/64$. We reveal scalar chiral order at half filling and kinetic ferromagnetism upon electron doping, with the latter directly compared to ultracold atom experiments. We further extend the stoMPS method to compute finite-temperature quantum dynamics, as demonstrated by the optical conductivity of the Hubbard model. We showcase the generalization of stoPEPS on up to $20\times20$ square-lattice quantum Ising model, where accurate results are obtained near its quantum critical point. Our method combines high sampling efficiency with full symmetry acceleration. The resulting state-of-the-art framework captures both equilibrium and dynamical properties down to ultralow temperatures, thereby providing a powerful theoretical tool for correlated quantum systems, particularly fermion Hubbard quantum gas microscopy.

papers.summary: Ultracold quantum gases offer a controllable and microscopically accessible platform for understanding and engineering superfluidity. papers.abstract: Ultracold quantum gases offer a controllable and microscopically accessible platform for understanding and engineering superfluidity. Yet, realizing a superleak that selectively transports the superfluid while suppressing normal flow has remained elusive. Here, we harness an optical superlattice to realize such a superleak through dynamical selectivity. The superfluid undergoes coherent Josephson transport, whereas the normal component exhibits slow, thermodynamically limited response, resulting in a flow-rate contrast of 500(49). Exploiting this contrast, we demonstrate repeated filtering of the normal component and dynamical purification of the superfluid, while sustaining coherent driven oscillations for up to 100 cycles. Our results establish a controllable atomic superleak and open possibilities for manipulating transport and thermodynamics in quantum fluids.

papers.abstract: We study the emergence of superconductivity in the one-band Hubbard model using the spin-rotation-invariant Kotliar-Ruckenstein slave-boson (SB) approach. Motivated by its intrinsically renormalized mean-field ground state, we construct an effective pairing vertex from dynamical fluctuations about the saddle point. Solving the anisotropic, frequency-dependent gap equation on the square lattice, we map the pairing instabilities across doping, interaction, temperature and real-frequency gap structure that qualitatively match experimental cuprate observations. This framework merges strong-correlation SB-type renormalizations with RPA-type pairing transparency, providing a scalable route to modeling multi-orbital superconductivity at strong coupling.

papers.abstract: Binary tree states have been introduced as compact correlated pair wave functions that improve upon the antisymmetrized geminal power by adding variational flexibility. Here, we extend the binary tree state to the fermionic half-filled Hubbard model using restricted and unrestricted orbitals. Although the ansatz is seniority zero in its optimized pairing basis, its expansion in the original Hubbard site basis can contain nonzero site- seniority character, while unrestricted orbital optimization provides additional flexibility through independent spin-up and spin-down orbitals. This provides a mechanism for a paired ansatz to describe the singly occupied configurations that dominate the repulsive Hubbard model at large U/t. papers.title: What Becomes of the Antiferromagnetic String When Long Range Neel Order Is Lost? Exact Results
papers.authors: Yuri DiMaggio
papers.summary_en: The paper investigates the fate of the antiferromagnetic string mechanistic description when long-range Néel order is lost but short-range correlations survive.
papers.summary: Early string descriptions of doped antiferromagnets associate hole motion in a locally Néel-ordered background with a path-dependent antiferromagnetic string. We ask what becomes of this mechanism when long range Néel order is lost while short range antiferromagnetic correlations persist. In a singlet bond representation, the underlying basis states do not assign an oriented \(A/B\) spin registrat
papers.abstract: Early string descriptions of doped antiferromagnets associate hole motion in a locally Néel-ordered background with a path-dependent antiferromagnetic string. We ask what becomes of this mechanism when long range Néel order is lost while short range antiferromagnetic correlations persist. In a singlet bond representation, the underlying basis states do not assign an oriented \(A/B\) spin registration to each bond. Therefore, any surviving long wavelength antiferromagnetic axis is naturally described as a director, \(\mathbf n\sim-\mathbf n\). Long range Néel order can nevertheless provide a global \(S^2\) lift of this director field; when that long range registration is lost, non liftable configurations of the \(RP^2\) manifold become physically accessible, opening a topologically nontrivial \(\mathbb Z_2\) sector. Its elementary defects are half vortices that globally minimize the \(RP^2\) \(σ\)-model energy within the nontrivial \(\mathbb Z_2\) sector. An \textit{a posteriori} energetic comparison further shows that the projective half vortex texture is softer than the corresponding vector reference texture. A pair of half vortices with opposite windings is logarithmically confined, \(V(R) = κ\ln\left(R/r_{\text{core}}\right)\), \(κ= πρ_s /2\). The resulting confinement is carried not by a one dimensional string but by an extended two-dimensional spin texture. Thus, the loss of long-range Néel order does not eliminate antiferromagnetic confinement but removes the global Néel lift. This activates a distinct projective mechanism in which a local path dependent string is replaced, at long wavelengths, by a global topological texture with logarithmic confinement.

papers.abstract: Group IV color centers in diamond -- silicon, germanium, tin, and lead-vacancy centers -- are a promising platform for quantum networking. Typical Group-IV creation utilizes ion implantation during diamond growth that leaves the color centers with a broad depth distribution and damage-induced strain inhomogeneity. Deterministic placement and damage reduction in Group IV generation are essential for improving this platform. In this letter, we report on the localization of germanium-vacancy (GeV$^-$) to a $<$ 10 nm layer via the timed injection of GeH$_4$ during microwave plasma chemical vapor deposition. In this layer we have realized 17 ppm of Ge and a strain-free environment for the GeV$^-$. Subsequent electron irradiation and annealing have generated a sheet density of 0.12 GeV$^-$/$μ$m$^2$. The minimal damage from color center generation mitigates spectral inhomogeneity and allows spectral resolution of isotopic clusters, with the best cluster having an inhomogeneous distribution of 2.14 GHz and an average linewidth of $47 \pm 11$ MHz. Our study gives insight into formation dynamics of GeV$^-$ in delta-doped systems and estimates our vacancy to GeV$^-$ yield to be $\geq$ 90%, establishing an athermal nearest-neighbor formation model. We further characterized the spin $T_2^*$ and set a lower bound of 730 ns, limited by a paramagnetic defect.

papers.title: Discrete time liquids
papers.authors: Zuo Wang, Paul M. Schindler, Marin Bukov, Marios H. Michael
papers.summary_en: This paper identifies a new spatiotemporal ordered phase called discrete time liquids featuring short-range temporal coherence due to time-solitons, distinct from discrete time crystals that exhibit robust long-range coherence.
papers.summary: Discrete time crystals exhibit robust subharmonic oscillations, spontaneously breaking the discrete time-translation symmetry of a periodic drive. Since their emergence, the question of whether other types of temporal many-body order can exist has attracted considerable attention. Here we identify discrete time liquids -- a new form of spatiotemporal order characterized by short-range temporal coh
papers.abstract: Discrete time crystals exhibit robust subharmonic oscillations, spontaneously breaking the discrete time-translation symmetry of a periodic drive. Since their emergence, the question of whether other types of temporal many-body order can exist has attracted considerable attention. Here we identify discrete time liquids -- a new form of spatiotemporal order characterized by short-range temporal coherence as a result of time-solitons. We study a two-dimensional spin system coupled to a finite-temperature cavity, whose fluctuations provide a noisy, approximately periodic drive with only finite temporal coherence. Remarkably, the spins nevertheless form a metastable state with robust period-doubled dynamics over an extended parameter regime. Unlike a time crystal, this state has only finite temporal coherence: individual trajectories stochastically switch between the two symmetry-related temporal configurations of the period-doubled response. We identify these switches as time-solitons: topological defects in temporal order that preserve local period doubling while destroying long-range temporal coherence, thereby producing the time liquid state. We propose a minimal model which reproduces the distribution of temporal correlations of the many-body system, suggesting a general description of the time liquid as a time crystal with a finite density of time-solitons. Because these solitons can occur at arbitrary times, ensemble averaging restores continuous time-translation symmetry, raising the intriguing possibility that discrete time liquids can exist in thermal equilibrium.

papers.authors: A. Bhattacharyay
papers.summary_en: This article revisits Einstein's diffusion theory, highlighting that non-Fickian diffusion with space-dependent diffusivity can also be normal diffusion, contrary to common assumptions.
papers.summary: Einstein's theory of diffusion defines what is considered {\it normal diffusion}. Historically, Einstein considered homogeneous diffusion characterised by a diffusion constant in his original calculations, resulting in what is known as {\it Fickian} diffusion, which thermally relaxes concentration inhomogeneities. However, in the same derivation of Einstein, the seed of generalisation of the theor
papers.abstract: Einstein's theory of diffusion defines what is considered {\it normal diffusion}. Historically, Einstein considered homogeneous diffusion characterised by a diffusion constant in his original calculations, resulting in what is known as {\it Fickian} diffusion, which thermally relaxes concentration inhomogeneities. However, in the same derivation of Einstein, the seed of generalisation of the theory to {\it non-Fickian} diffusion in the presence of space-dependent diffusivity is hidden. This indicates that non-Fickian diffusion, which can drive concentration inhomogeneities, can also be normal diffusion. The present article discusses the origin of the {\it normal} non-Fickian diffusion in Einstein's theory of diffusion.
papers.physics_advance: Demonstration that non-Fickian diffusion (with spatially varying diffusivity) can be a type of normal diffusion embedded already in Einstein’s diffusion theory.

papers.authors: Edilberto O. Silva
papers.summary_en: This paper studies a finite-width 2D quantum ring with a d-wave altermagnetic term, confinement potential, magnetic field, and Aharonov-Bohm flux, revealing angular-channel mixing effects, shell oscillations, and persistent charge currents, but no persistent spin current.

The altermagnetic interaction mixes $m$ and $m\pm2$ angular channels while preserving their parity. Circular symmetry renders the crystal orientation spectrally irrelevant and makes the two sp
papers.abstract: We study a finite-width two-dimensional quantum ring with a quadratic $d$-wave altermagnetic term, Tan--Inkson confinement, a perpendicular magnetic field, and independently tunable Aharonov--Bohm (AB) flux. The altermagnetic interaction mixes $m$ and $m\pm2$ angular channels while preserving their parity. Circular symmetry renders the crystal orientation spectrally irrelevant and makes the two spin blocks exactly isospectral. The resulting same-parity anticrossings are resolved at low filling, and multichannel mixing is found near the Fermi level of highly occupied rings. Independent converged calculations for $N_e=1400$ and $1800$ establish the reconstructed Fermi edge and magnetic response in a finite field window and the persistent current over a full AB flux period. The analytic conventional reference separates radial-subband depopulation (dHvA-type cycles) from finer finite-ring shell oscillations; we do not assign a global Fourier spectrum to unverified altermagnetic field scans. The few-electron thermal response is obtained from an exact fixed-particle-number canonical partition function, avoiding finite-system errors of a fixed-mean-number approximation. The circular model supports an equilibrium charge current but no persistent spin current.

papers.authors: Sebastian Alois Fuchs, Enrico Arrigoni, Tommaso Maria Mazzocchi
papers.summary_en: This work presents a fit-error correction methodology for the auxiliary master equation approach (AMEA) used in low-temperature nonequilibrium DMFT calculations to improve accuracy of the self-energy.

papers.abstract: The auxiliary master equation approach (AMEA) is a nonperturbative impurity solver for steady-state nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). It replaces the physical hybridization function by that of a small auxiliary open quantum system, whose parameters are fitted to reproduce it, and then solves the resulting many-body problem essentially exactly. AMEA's accuracy is thus limited by the quality of this fit: since the fastest-varying part of the hybridization is set by the distribution function, whose Fermi edges sharpen at low temperature, the fit tends to overestimate the temperature, especially for weak reservoir coupling. For the auxiliary hybridization itself, however, AMEA's self-energy is essentially exact. We correct for the fit error by estimating, via an approximate solver applicable to arbitrary hybridization functions, the ratio between the self-energies of the physical and auxiliary hybridizations, and using it to extend AMEA's self-energy from the auxiliary to the physical case. This fit-error correction becomes exact whenever either the fit or the approximate solver is exact. We benchmark the scheme using the nonequilibrium Kajueter-Kotliar iterated perturbation theory (IPT), generalized here to spin-polarized solutions, as the approximate solver; other approximate solvers, such as the noncrossing approximation, can be used as well. Applied to an Anderson impurity model with a spin-polarized bath, and within DMFT to a Hubbard layer weakly coupled to two metallic reservoirs, the correction largely removes the spurious heating from the AMEA fit and from insufficient thermalization by the reservoirs, while preserving the correct description of the Mott insulator, which IPT alone cannot fully recover.

papers.abstract: Phonon-mediated nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer (RET) in metal deuterides is severely constrained by inertial rest-mass dilution, lattice fracture limits, and thermal nuclear spin cancellation. Extending the generalized nuclear Dicke model to Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) magnons eliminates mass dilution via hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling while unlocking relativistic Dirac M2 coupling via Overhauser spin polarization. papers.authors: Jishad Kumar, Achilleas Lazarides, Tapio Ala-Nissila
papers.summary_en: This work studies coherence and transport in fermionic two-bath quantum reset dynamics, showing that exact replacement of bath occupations while preserving system-bath coherences is unphysical. Instead, they construct a two-reservoir protocol with number-conserving thermal attenuators ensuring complete positivity and fermionic admissibility.
papers.summary: Coherence preservation and environmental renewal offer competing ways of controlling quantum memory and transport. We show that a seemingly natural protocol which exactly replaces the bath occupations while preserving arbitrary system--bath coherences need not correspond to a physical fermionic state. We instead construct a two-reservoir protocol with independent, number-conserving thermal attenua
papers.abstract: Coherence preservation and environmental renewal offer competing ways of controlling quantum memory and transport. We show that a seemingly natural protocol which exactly replaces the bath occupations while preserving arbitrary system--bath coherences need not correspond to a physical fermionic state. We instead construct a two-reservoir protocol with independent, number-conserving thermal attenuators, for which complete positivity and fermionic admissibility hold by construction. Physical attenuation necessarily modifies bath populations as well as cross correlations; the coherence control is not an independent hard-reset knob. Quadratic dynamics reduces the stroboscopic problem to an exact matrix fixed-point equation without a weak-coupling or Markov approximation. Analytically, coherence retention enhances the leading short-cycle transfer rate, including the complete-erasure limit; no general endpoint-vanishing theorem exists. An exact stationary continuity theorem forces the through-current to vanish whenever either reservoir is left entirely unrefreshed, although no analogous theorem suppresses it at complete erasure. For biased structured reservoirs, exact finite-chain calculations display distinct coherence-, current-, and signed energy-transfer operating points; a resolved high-retention boundary layer exposes strong finite-size sensitivity of the coherence peak. The model provides a microscopic, fermion-admissible benchmark for the interplay of reservoir coherence, particle transport, and energetic exchange.

papers.summary_en: This study elucidates how nitrogen vacancies influence ferroelectric domain growth and coercive field in AlN, reconciling discrepancies between theoretical and experimental observations.
papers.summary: Aluminum nitride-based ferroelectrics combine high remanent polarization, thermal stability, weak size effects, a wide bandgap and back-end process compatibility, making them promising for high density non-volatile memory. However, their high coercive field ($E_\mathrm{c}$) and unclear polarization switching mechanism limit further applications. Theoretical predictions indicate preferential revers
papers.abstract: Aluminum nitride-based ferroelectrics combine high remanent polarization, thermal stability, weak size effects, a wide bandgap and back-end process compatibility, making them promising for high density non-volatile memory. However, their high coercive field ($E_\mathrm{c}$) and unclear polarization switching mechanism limit further applications. Theoretical predictions indicate preferential reversed domain growth along the polar axis, whereas experiments show nearly isotropic growth or preferential growth perpendicular to this axis. Here, we combine density functional theory, Deep Potential molecular dynamics and experimental characterization to determine how nitrogen vacancies ($V_\mathrm{N}$) regulate domain growth and $E_\mathrm{c}$. In ideal crystal, strong lattice coupling along the polar axis drives preferential domain growth in this direction. $V_\mathrm{N}$ locally weakens this coupling and promotes polarization nucleation. The spatial distribution of $V_\mathrm{N}$ and the temporal sequence of vacancy induced switching jointly determine the direction and morphology of reversed domain growth. We further show that scandium doping promotes $V_\mathrm{N}$ formation, thereby enhancing defect mediated nucleation and reducing $E_\mathrm{c}$. These findings establish a multiscale mechanism governing thin-film domain-growth kinetics and macroscopic $E_\mathrm{c}$, reconciling experimental observations with ideal crystal simulations and providing defect engineering principles for low-voltage, reliable and scalable ferroelectric devices.

papers.title: Non-adiabatic Optimisation via Localisation-Delocalisation Transitions
papers.authors: Ryan Smith, Sabrina Yue Wang, Filippo Maria Gambetta, Raul A. Santos
papers.summary_en: The authors propose a quantum optimization algorithm leveraging localization-delocalization transitions via continuous reverse annealing to accelerate solving classical spin-glass problems.
papers.summary: The promise of efficiently solving classical optimisation problems on quantum computers is tantalizing. As many such problems can be mapped to approximating the ground state of spin-glasses, paradigmatic models for studying many-body localisation, it is natural to ask if some of the intuition coming from quantum statistical mechanics can help guide the construction of novel quantum optimisation al
papers.abstract: The promise of efficiently solving classical optimisation problems on quantum computers is tantalizing. As many such problems can be mapped to approximating the ground state of spin-glasses, paradigmatic models for studying many-body localisation, it is natural to ask if some of the intuition coming from quantum statistical mechanics can help guide the construction of novel quantum optimisation algorithms. In this work, we discuss how continuous reverse quantum annealing crossing a many-body localisation transition can be accelerated by considering the density of Landau-Zener crossings as the system is quenched. We provide an interpretation of this behaviour in terms of an effective Fokker-Planck equation for the success probability of the algorithm. This interpretation suggests an improvement in the required annealing time as a function of the system size $N$, which goes from $\mathcal{O}({\rm poly}(N))$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for reference states with non-vanishing energy density. We show that the continuous dynamics can be Trotterised with a number of steps that remains modest as system size increases, making it appealing for near-term devices. For the resulting circuit implementation, we provide a quantitative strategy for determining the parameters of the time-dependent Hamiltonian. We compare the performance of our digitised algorithm, which we call FRIO, against that of the QAOA for finding the ground state of spin-glass problems, in particular the SK model. The numerical results suggest that with suitably selected circuit parameters which can be efficiently found using thermalizing dynamics, FRIO almost always outperforms the conventional QAOA ansatz with pre-optimized angles.

papers.title: Order-Disorder in Fe-Si Alloys: Implications for Seismic and Transport Properties of Earth's Inner Core
papers.authors: Cong Liu, Xin Deng, R. E. Cohen
papers.summary_en: This theoretical study models Fe-Si alloys under Earth's inner-core conditions, revealing phase coexistence and order-dependent anisotropic elastic and transport properties relevant for seismic interpretations.
papers.summary: Understanding the structure and dynamics of Earth's inner core is essential for constraining its composition, thermal evolution, and seismic behavior. Silicon is widely considered a major light element in the core. Here, we use first-principles molecular dynamics and thermodynamic modeling to investigate the structural, elastic, and transport properties of iron-silicon (Fe-Si) alloys under inner-c
papers.abstract: Understanding the structure and dynamics of Earth's inner core is essential for constraining its composition, thermal evolution, and seismic behavior. Silicon is widely considered a major light element in the core. Here, we use first-principles molecular dynamics and thermodynamic modeling to investigate the structural, elastic, and transport properties of iron-silicon (Fe-Si) alloys under inner-core conditions. By computing the Gibbs free energies of multiple solid phases, including ordered B2, hexagonal close-packed (hcp), face-centered cubic (fcc), and body-centered cubic (bcc) Fe-Si, we construct a phase diagram relevant to inner-core pressures and temperatures. We identify a pronounced miscibility gap between hcp and cubic Fe--Si phases, with phase coexistence over approximately 6--11 wt\% Si at 6000 K. The cubic phase exhibits a strong order-dependent elastic response, with disordered bcc showing a large intrinsic shear anisotropy (22.9\% at 6000 K), in contrast to the nearly isotropic hcp phase (0.6\%). Meanwhile, disordered bcc Fe--Si produces shear wave velocities ($V_S=3.73$ km$\cdot$s$^{-1}$) and Poisson's ratios comparable with seismological constraints. In addition, disordered bcc Fe--Si exhibits a lower thermal conductivity than hcp Fe--Si, providing a quantitative constraint on phase-dependent electronic heat transport. These results demonstrate that chemical ordering strongly controls the stability and physical properties of cubic Fe--Si alloys, and suggest that metastable or localized cubic Fe--Si phases may contribute to the structural and transport complexity of Earth's inner core.

We show that a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle can use this structure as a thermodynamic probe, revealing which parts of the spectrum become dynamically accessible and thermodynamically relevant during a driven transformation. papers.abstract: Quasiperiodic systems combine sharply different spectral and localisation regimes with a dense hierarchy of dynamical time scales. We show that a finite-rate quantum Otto cycle can use this structure as a thermodynamic probe, revealing which parts of the spectrum become dynamically accessible and thermodynamically relevant during a driven transformation. For a generalised Aubry-André-Harper chain, the resulting response is not determined by the static quasiperiodic regime alone: extended, near-critical, and crossing protocols do not exhibit universal ordering of work fluctuations. Instead, the statistics reflect transition pathways that are simultaneously dynamically coupled, thermally occupied, and energetically significant. The same spectral accessibility separates thermodynamic recovery from microscopic adiabatic recovery. Positive mean work can reappear while the population transfer dynamics remain strongly nonadiabatic because finite-rate population transfer is redistributed toward energetically less costly channels rather than suppressed. The full work distribution reveals a further separation, with a finite rate window in which positive-work cycles form a majority although the mean work remains negative. This behaviour persists in finite-size analysis. A thermally weighted spectral susceptibility connects these effects to a distributed hierarchy of dynamically active spectral regions rather than to a single minimum-gap bottleneck. Finite thermal contacts preserve this picture while introducing a second time scale and intercycle memory. Quantum Otto cycles can therefore provide a fluctuation-resolved thermodynamic probe of quasiperiodic spectral accessibility, complementary to direct spectroscopic and eigenstate-resolved diagnostics.

papers.authors: Jerome Lloyd, Dmitry A. Abanin
papers.summary_en: The authors present a simple algorithm for preparing quantum thermal states on near-term quantum processors, achieving an error scaling of order squared system-bath coupling strength.
papers.summary: Preparation of quantum thermal states of many-body systems is a key computational challenge for quantum processors, with applications in physics, chemistry, and classical optimization. We provide a simple and efficient algorithm for thermal state preparation, combining engineered bath resetting and modulated system-bath coupling to derive a quantum channel approximately satisfying quantum detailed
papers.abstract: Preparation of quantum thermal states of many-body systems is a key computational challenge for quantum processors, with applications in physics, chemistry, and classical optimization. We provide a simple and efficient algorithm for thermal state preparation, combining engineered bath resetting and modulated system-bath coupling to derive a quantum channel approximately satisfying quantum detailed balance relations. We show that the fixed point $\hatσ$ of the channel approximates the Gibbs state as $\|\hatσ-\hatσ_β\|\sim θ^2$, where $θ$ is the system-bath coupling and $\hatσ_β\propto e^{-β\hat H_S}$. We provide extensive numerics, for the example of the 2D Quantum Ising model, confirming that the protocol successfully prepares the thermal state throughout the finite-temperature phase diagram, including near the quantum phase transition. Simulations for free-fermion systems provide further evidence for the accuracy of the protocol for large system sizes in the weak-coupling limit. Our algorithm provides a path to efficient quantum simulation of quantum-correlated states at finite temperature with current and near-term quantum processors.

papers.abstract: Thermal state preparation is a central challenge in the simulation of quantum many-body systems. Yet, provably efficient algorithms for this task were only introduced recently [Chen et al. Nature 646, 561 (2025)]. These algorithms are based on dissipative Lindbladian evolution which exactly fixes the thermal state. Controlled and efficient digital simulation of this evolution, although possible in principle, remains out of reach for present-day quantum hardware. Subsequent work has therefore focused on analog approximations of the proposed Lindbladians via `collision models' with relatively modest requirements -- a resettable bath of ancilla qubits whose couplings to the system can be tuned in time-dependent fashion -- while still admitting rigorous fixed-point error bounds. Existing rigorous approaches, however, do not exploit the fact that these constructions generically implement not only the desired Lindblad dynamics, but also an additional unitary evolution generated by the system Hamiltonian which may aid convergence to the thermal state [Lloyd and Abanin arXiv:2506.21318 (2025)]. Here, we show that this unitary contribution does indeed tighten the fixed-point error bound and demonstrate that it is rigorously controlled by the system-bath coupling strength $J$, scaling as $J^2$. This demonstrates that the effect of the spurious `Lamb shift' term generated by the system-bath interaction can be controlled by tuning $J$. We clarify the role, previously observed, of a randomized implementation in suppressing possible resonances of the drive with the many-body spectrum, and bound the additional variance that this randomization imposes on observables. Finally, we numerically study aspects of the protocol which are relevant for its practical realization, such as the mixing time.

papers.summary_en: This paper develops a comprehensive framework for screening strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for solid oxide fuel and electrolysis cells using quantum computing. It integrates electronic structure embedding methods with continuum device modeling to link microscopic quantum observables to engineering metrics and estimates the potential industrial impact.
papers.summary: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observab
papers.abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

papers.authors: Chenhang Xu, Patrick Liu, Bo Zhang, Minyong Han, Henry G. Bell, Cameron J. R. Duncan, Yusong Liu, Patrick L. Kramer, Randy Lemons, Jake D. Koralek, Alexander H. Reid, Dong Qian, Harold Y. Hwang, Alfred Zong

papers.summary: Quantum materials are characterized by intertwined orders, and a fundamental goal in condensed matter physics is to achieve their selective control in such a way that one order parameter can be tuned while leaving others largely unaffected. Although significant progress has been made in thermal equilibrium, realizing such control out of equilibrium remains highly challenging. Here we employed in-s
papers.abstract: Quantum materials are characterized by intertwined orders, and a fundamental goal in condensed matter physics is to achieve their selective control in such a way that one order parameter can be tuned while leaving others largely unaffected. Although significant progress has been made in thermal equilibrium, realizing such control out of equilibrium remains highly challenging. Here we employed in-situ tensile strain to selectively manipulate the photoinduced lattice dynamics associated with ferroelectric and magnetic orders in multiferroic BiFeO$_3$. By applying MeV ultrafast electron diffraction to freestanding BiFeO$_3$ membranes under tunable strain, we showed that tensile strain markedly suppresses the ultrafast photoinduced reduction of the ferroelectric displacement. By contrast, the photoinduced dynamics of the antiferrodistortive rotation of the oxygen octahedra, which modulates the magnetic order, remains insensitive to strain. Not only do these findings reveal distinct microscopic pathways underlying nonequilibrium multiferroic dynamics, they also establish tunable strain as an effective route for engineering ultrafast phase control in correlated materials.

papers.title: Spin polarization in a chiral ladder: elastic and inelastic environments
papers.authors: D. T. Verrilli H., Jorge Cardenas-Gamboa, Mayra Peralta, Claudia Felser, José H. Garcia, Solmar Varela, Nelson Bolívar
papers.summary_en: This paper investigates spin polarization transmitted through a two-leg chiral ladder model with time-reversal-invariant spin-orbit coupling, analyzing how transport window and environmental probe types affect integrated spin currents.
papers.summary: We study how the transport window and environmental reinjection determine the spin polarization transmitted through a minimal two-leg chiral ladder. The model contains time-reversal-invariant helical spin--orbit coupling, spin-independent interchain hopping, and nonmagnetic contacts with two orbital modes per lead. Sublattice symmetry makes the coherent spin-transmission kernel exactly odd in ener
papers.abstract: We study how the transport window and environmental reinjection determine the spin polarization transmitted through a minimal two-leg chiral ladder. The model contains time-reversal-invariant helical spin--orbit coupling, spin-independent interchain hopping, and nonmagnetic contacts with two orbital modes per lead. Sublattice symmetry makes the coherent spin-transmission kernel exactly odd in energy. A window centered on the symmetry point therefore gives zero integrated spin current, whereas a displaced window selects an uncanceled spectral interval. The resulting polarization reverses between enantiomers and vanishes in the decoupled-chain, zero-spin--orbit, and equivalent-strand limits of this model. We compare uniform absorption, energy-resolved elastic probes, and thermalized voltage probes at the same finite bias, including reinjection whenever probes are present. Charge conservation alone does not prohibit enhancement of the integrated spin signal: the elastic-probe response can increase at finite bias even where its linear-response counterpart decreases. Thermalized probes can also lift the centered-window zero that elastic probes preserve. Absorption and reinjection also change the transmitted charge, so enhancement of spin current and enhancement of normalized polarization must be distinguished. Static onsite disorder produces sample-dependent fluctuations; its signed ensemble mean is reported with uncertainty and is not forced to vanish in a displaced window. These results identify the energy interval and reservoir prescription that must be controlled when interpreting dephasing trends in minimal models relevant to chirality-induced spin selectivity.

papers.summary_en: This work investigates how strain affects the transient diffusion and photoluminescence of dark excitons in hBN-encapsulated WSe2 monolayers at cryogenic temperatures, showing tensile strain increases hot exciton excess energy and diffusion by suppressing bright-to-dark scattering.
papers.summary: Tungsten-based transition metal dichalcogenides exhibit dark excitons as the energetically lowest states. These are crucial for exciton thermalization and propagation and they dominate low-temperature photoluminescence via the emergence of pronounced phonon sidebands. After a resonant excitation, highly mobile hot dark excitons are formed, which quickly thermalize into an equilibrium distribution.
papers.abstract: Tungsten-based transition metal dichalcogenides exhibit dark excitons as the energetically lowest states. These are crucial for exciton thermalization and propagation and they dominate low-temperature photoluminescence via the emergence of pronounced phonon sidebands. After a resonant excitation, highly mobile hot dark excitons are formed, which quickly thermalize into an equilibrium distribution. The application of strain modifies the exciton energy landscape and, in particular, the relative energy separation between bright and dark exciton states. The impact of strain on the transient photoluminescence and diffusion of non-equilibrium excitons has remained largely unexplored so far. In this work, we investigate the spatiotemporal exciton dynamics in strained hBN-encapsulated WSe2 monolayers at cryogenic temperatures. We demonstrate that tensile strain abruptly increases the excess energy of hot excitons, thereby accelerating their transient diffusion. We trace this back to suppressed phonon-mediated scattering from bright to dark excitons. Furthermore, we predict a periodic modulation of the transient exciton diffusion in the presence of a compressive strain resulting from strain-driven emission of M phonons. The gained microscopic insights illustrate how strain can be used to engineer transient photoluminescence and exciton diffusion in technologically promising 2D semiconductors.

papers.abstract: In this work we theoretically study the structural transformations occurring in monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) subjected to strong deformations. The first-principle computer simulations are based on the density functional theory employing the pseudopotentials with the exchange-correlation energy given in Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof form. Depending on the direction and the type of the strain, the simulations reveal different types of structural transformations in two-dimensional (2D) h-BN associated with the elastic failure. It is found that, under certain shear strains, there can form an ordered 2D orthorhombic phase with the 2D layer space symmetry pmmm. Thermal stability of the latter up to ~900 K is demonstrated by first-principle Born-Oppenheimer molecular dynamics. The examination of electronic structure indicates that, in contrast to the conventional h-BN, which is an insulator with the wide band gap, the predicted orthorhombic phase is expected to be a semiconductor with the narrow band gap of ~ 0.65 eV.

It is not mentioned in well-known condensed-matter textbook. Here, we review its origi
papers.abstract: Formulated a hundred years ago, the Bridgman formula for thermal conductivity of liquids postulates a proportionality between sound velocity and thermal conductivity. This designates phonons as heat carriers in a liquid. Its empirical success has been under-appreciated and its conceptual implications overlooked. It is not mentioned in well-known condensed-matter textbook. Here, we review its origin, its links to hydrodynamic Euler equations and to the fundamental paradox surrounding the parabolic heat equation and its fate across the quantum-classical crossover.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation with Quantum Feedback
papers.authors: Ryotaro Honma, Tan Van Vu
papers.summary_en: This work derives a finite-time thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR) for open quantum systems under continuous monitoring and Markovian feedback, linking current fluctuations, entropy production, and mutual information.
papers.summary: Fluctuations are intrinsic to microscopic systems and impose fundamental limits on nonequilibrium precision, as captured by the thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR), which links current fluctuations to entropy production. While feedback control is expected to further suppress fluctuations, its role within the TUR framework has remained unclear, particularly in quantum systems where control is
papers.abstract: Fluctuations are intrinsic to microscopic systems and impose fundamental limits on nonequilibrium precision, as captured by the thermodynamic uncertainty relation (TUR), which links current fluctuations to entropy production. While feedback control is expected to further suppress fluctuations, its role within the TUR framework has remained unclear, particularly in quantum systems where control is inherently information-driven. In this Letter, we consider open quantum systems weakly coupled to a thermal environment, in which quantum jumps are continuously monitored, and Markovian feedback is applied. Using quantum mutual information to quantify the information contribution induced by feedback, we derive a finite-time TUR for arbitrary time-integrated currents in terms of entropy production and mutual information. Our results uncover how feedback control suppresses fluctuations together with thermodynamic cost and establish a fundamental precision bound imposed by information-based control. As an application, we analyze a quantum clock model and demonstrate that the clock precision can be enhanced by feedback control in the presence of a single thermal reservoir.

papers.abstract: We introduce graphene nanohelicoids, geometric analogs of graphene nanoribbons, in which the honeycomb lattice is embedded on a helicoidal surface. Starting from the three-dimensional helical structure, we construct effective one-dimensional lattice models with band structures characterized by a momentum-shifted particle-hole relation $E_v(k)=-E_c(k+π)$ that reflects an antichiral symmetry arising from the nonsymmorphic symmetry. A systematic investigation of graphene nanohelicoids using the tight-binding approximation reveals a number of trends upon varying width and edge orientation, for instance, alternating transitions between semiconducting and metallic regimes. As the structure width varies, the band gap periodically closes and reopens, accompanied by an alternating Zak phase that switches between trivial and nontrivial. Using an analytic tight-binding model with a continuous deformation of the graphene nanohelicoids, we explain the origin of width- and termination-dependent band inversion and alternating Zak phase, and derive the relationship between the termination-resolved index and the sublattice symmetry operator in one-dimensional nonsymmorphic systems.
papers.physics_advance: Discovery of antichiral symmetry and width-dependent topological band inversion in graphene nanohelicoids.

papers.summary_zh: 本文提出石墨烯纳米螺旋体，作为镶嵌在螺旋曲面上的纳米带的几何类似物，揭示其能带结构中的反手性对称性，表明宽度和边缘方向变化导致电子结构周期性地在半导体和金属态之间转换，并伴随带隙闭合和Zak相交替变化。

papers.result_en: They find alternating transitions between semiconducting and metallic regimes as width varies, periodic band gap closings with alternating Zak phase switching between trivial and nontrivial topologies, explained by band inversion dependent on width and termination.
papers.result_zh: 研究发现随着宽度变化，石墨烯纳米螺旋体在半导体和金属态间交替转换，带隙周期性关闭并伴随Zak相在平凡和非平凡拓扑间切换，这由带反转和边界终止决定。

papers.future_zh: 未来研究方向可能包括实现石墨烯纳米螺旋体的实验制备，研究其拓扑相相关的输运和光学性质，以及考虑相互作用和无序的模型扩展。

papers.authors: Gerhard Jung
papers.summary_en: Two non-Markovian coarse-grained models derived from a linear nonequilibrium system with a tagged particle coupled to oscillators exhibit distinct behaviors under external forces.
papers.summary: We investigate two different types of non-Markovian coarse-grained models extracted from a linear, non-equilibrium microscopic system, featuring a tagged particle coupled to underdamped oscillators. papers.abstract: We investigate two different types of non-Markovian coarse-grained models extracted from a linear, non-equilibrium microscopic system, featuring a tagged particle coupled to underdamped oscillators. The first model is obtained by analytically ``integrating out'' the oscillators and the second is based on a derivation using projection operator techniques. We observe that these two models behave very differently when the tagged particle is exposed to external harmonic potentials or pulling forces. Most importantly, we find that the analytic model has a well defined friction kernel and can be used to extract work, consistent with the microscopic system, while the projection model corresponds to an effective equilibrium model, which cannot be used to extract work. We apply the analysis to two popular non-equilibrium systems, time-delay feedback control and the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Finally, we highlight that our study could have important consequences for dynamic coarse-graining of non-equilibrium systems going far beyond the linear systems investigated in this manuscript.

papers.title: Shear-induced mechanical yielding controls cluster morphology and dynamics in aggregating non-Brownian suspensions
papers.authors: Jae Hwan Jeong, Donald L. Koch, Sarah Hormozi
papers.summary_en: This study elucidates how shear flow controls cluster formation, morphology, rotational dynamics, and stress generation in aggregating non-Brownian suspensions with dominant interparticle attraction.
papers.summary: In sheared aggregating suspensions, flow drives both the formation and breakage of particle clusters, whose dynamic evolution influences transport and rheological properties. papers.abstract: In sheared aggregating suspensions, flow drives both the formation and breakage of particle clusters, whose dynamic evolution influences transport and rheological properties. Understanding these mechanisms remains challenging due to the complex interplay between interparticle forces, hydrodynamic interactions, and shear flow. Using parallelized Accelerated Stokesian Dynamics (PASD) simulations, we investigate cluster microstructure and rotational dynamics, and how their coupling produces suspension stress in sheared, attractive non-Brownian suspensions. When interparticle attraction dominates over separating shear forces, clusters grow until mechanical loading balances maximum interparticle bond strength. We examine how the cluster stresslet depends on cluster size, with both quantities normalized by their mechanical yielding scales. Scaled cluster stresslets collapse onto a master curve exhibiting three distinct regimes: cubic, quadratic, and linear with respect to the scaled radius of gyration $R_g$. In the cubic regime, small, compact clusters behave as rigid bodies, whose hydrodynamic stresslet scales with cluster volume $R_g^3$. As clusters grow into the quadratic regime, low-aspect-ratio clusters preferentially yield under flow, driving a proportional increase in average aspect ratio with size. High-aspect-ratio clusters follow Jeffery rotational dynamics within the flow-gradient plane, spending longer durations aligned with the flow and thereby reducing their time-averaged hydrodynamic stresslet to scale as $R_g^2$. In the linear regime, clusters approach the maximum size sustainable by the interparticle bonds. The internal tension is bounded by the maximum bond strength, limiting the stresslet to an $R_g$ dependence. These findings establish a mechanistic framework connecting microscale cluster morphology and dynamics to macroscale rheology.
papers.physics_advance: Identification of distinct scaling regimes of cluster stresslets linked to cluster morphology and yielding phenomena in sheared attractive non-Brownian suspensions.
papers.relevance_reason: Provides new mechanistic understanding of cluster morphology, rotational dynamics, and their coupling to rheology in aggregating non-Brownian suspensions, revealing scaling laws and yielding regimes connecting microscale structure to macros

papers.method_en: Parallelized Accelerated Stokesian Dynamics simulations probe the size, shape, rotational behavior, and hydrodynamic stresslets of clusters under shear, normalized by mechanical yielding scales set by maximal bond strength.

papers.title: Supercoiling Drives DNA-Protein Co-Condensation
papers.authors: Sihan Liu, Hongbo Zhao, Andrej Košmrlj
papers.summary_en: This theoretical study shows that DNA supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for DNA-protein co-condensation by facilitating twist-to-writhe conversion and promoting protein wetting-induced capillary collapse.

papers.abstract: The co-condensation of DNA and proteins plays an important role in genome compaction, including heterochromatin formation and chromosome segregation. Meanwhile, transcription and replication continuously generate DNA supercoiling, yet how the resulting torsional stress affects co-condensation remains poorly understood. Here, by coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, we show that supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for co-condensation through a mutually reinforcing interplay with protein wetting. Specifically, protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, generating highly writhed DNA conformations that in turn promote capillary collapse into a protein-rich droplet. In the absence of supercoiling, DNA remains kinetically trapped in metastable extended states within our model, whereas sufficiently strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation. These results establish topology as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation and provide a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes can dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

papers.title: Symmetry-Preserving Local Representation for Short-Range Interaction in Complex Materials
papers.authors: Hao Cheng, Tong Yang, Hao Wu, Haokai Hong, Zhongrui Wang, Shu Ping Lau, Wanyu Lin, Kay Chen Tan, Ming Yang
papers.summary_en: A symmetry-preserving local representation framework is proposed to model short-range interactions in highly disordered materials, strictly enforcing topological continuity and translational invariance via boundary passivation. The approach is applied to high-entropy alloys, capturing nonlinear ligand effects and many-body interactions efficiently without explicit periodic expansion.

papers.abstract: Modeling short-range interactions in highly disordered materials remains challenging due to the immense configuration space and the disruption of local symmetry in truncated theoretical models. Here, we propose a symmetry-preserving local representation framework that strictly enforces topological continuity and translational invariance via boundary passivation. Applied to high-entropy alloys, this approach autonomously unravels the nonlinear ligand effects modulating local reactivity and accurately captures coverage-dependent many-body interactions without explicit periodic expansion. By resolving the conflict between localized chemical environments and extended periodic boundaries, this framework not only reduces computational complexity by an order of magnitude but also provides a physically transparent paradigm for deciphering short-range order in complex condensed matter systems.

papers.summary_zh: 提出了一种保持对称性的局部表征框架，通过边界钝化严格实现拓扑连续性与平移不变性，用于描述高度无序材料中的短程相互作用。应用于高熵合金，准确捕捉非线性配体效应和多体相互作用，且无需显式周期展开。

papers.title: Twisted scattering from Chern-Simons theory
papers.authors: Guillermo Arias-Tamargo, Philip Boyle Smith, Rishi Mouland, Max Velásquez Cotini Hutt
papers.summary_en: This paper constructs topological defects in 2D Dirac fermion systems preserving non-anomalous continuous symmetries acting differently on left- and right-movers, realized via Chern-Simons theory, and computes associated twist lines, boundary central charges, and SPT classes.
papers.summary: We consider boundary conditions of two-dimensional Dirac fermions which preserve a non-anomalous continuous symmetry which acts differently on the left- and right-movers. Such boundaries are equivalent to topological defects of Weyl fermions preserving the symmetry. We give a general construction of such defects for conformally-embedded symmetries using Chern-Simons theory. They always exist and c
papers.abstract: We consider boundary conditions of two-dimensional Dirac fermions which preserve a non-anomalous continuous symmetry which acts differently on the left- and right-movers. Such boundaries are equivalent to topological defects of Weyl fermions preserving the symmetry. We give a general construction of such defects for conformally-embedded symmetries using Chern-Simons theory. They always exist and can be realised as half-space gauging defects for some finite categorical symmetry. Using this technology, we compute the twist lines to which fermions become attached upon scattering through the defect, the boundary central charge of the corresponding folded boundary state, and its mod-2 valued SPT class. As applications, we first consider abelian symmetries and find agreement with known results in the literature. We then study a novel example where an $SU(2) \times SU(4) \times U(1)^2$ symmetry is preserved. In contrast to the abelian case, the twist lines are intrinsically non-invertible and belong to either a $\text{TY}(\mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_3)$ or $\text{Rep}(\mathbb{S}_3) \times \mathbb{Z}_3$ symmetry depending on whether scattering is to the left or the right.

papers.method_en: Using conformal embedding and categorical symmetry concepts, the authors realize defects as half-space gauging defects and employ Chern-Simons field theory to characterize scattering twists and boundary data.

papers.result_en: They identify twist lines that are non-invertible in a novel non-abelian symmetry example and reproduce known abelian cases, revealing rich structure in boundary scattering and symmetry-protected topological classifications.
